summary:
Western Sahara has no single legal order running through it. Morocco controls most of the ground, and Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate there. The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims sovereignty over the whole territory and governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria. Which framework a visitor stands under depends on which part of the territory they are in.

Moroccan jurisdiction is exercised in practice, not merely asserted. On 9 December 2005 Human Rights Watch reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The report documents Moroccan security services, courts and detention operating on Sahrawi political cases. The dossier records no comparable proceeding against Sahrawi activists after that date, so the 2005 case stands as historical evidence of how Moroccan authority is applied rather than as a description of current enforcement.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. In the areas Morocco controls, Moroccan law applies. Under the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, several catalogues of LGBT law (Council for Global Equality, Equaldex, ILGA) record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both males and females and punishable by up to three years in prison, and a July 2017 PinkNews roundup listed the territory as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and stated that it had been illegal there for decades. For a trans visitor, the operative question is how a relationship would be classified locally: a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls inside the prohibition as the sources describe it.

Detention on these charges has been documented in the camps. A 2009 USCRI report found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape.

No protection machinery is documented for either framework. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it', and CEAR concludes that this ambiguity leaves LGBTQ people without legal protection against discrimination or violence.

The sources describe most residents as Muslim and same-sex relationships as viewed as a foreign phenomenon, which bears on how a visible trans or gender-nonconforming visitor is likely to be received alongside the legal exposure.
tangentialFactors:
The region was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalised in Spain until 1979. Both dates sit after the transfer of the territory, and the sources present them as shaping the legal and social inheritance that local frameworks draw on.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic has been an African Union member since 2016, which gives the claimant government a measure of external recognition while its control on the ground remains limited to exile institutions and the camps in Algeria. Partial recognition affects which authorities a visitor could appeal to and which would answer.

Same-sex activity is also illegal in Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the SADR claims, so the two frameworks agree on criminalisation even where they differ on sovereignty. The 2010 constitutional statement by the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico sits against the 2009 finding of prisoners held on those charges in the camps, an internal contradiction in the claimant government's own position rather than a difference between the two frameworks.
localsOnly:
Residents of the camps and of Moroccan-controlled areas face exposure under whichever framework governs where they live: the sources record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both males and females in the SADR, punishable by up to three years in prison, and criminalised under Moroccan law in the areas Morocco controls.

Residents have no documented recourse. CEAR states there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence, and reads the Constitution's silence on the subject as leaving no legal protection either. The 2009 USCRI finding shows officials in the camps themselves detaining people on these charges.

Sahrawi political organising inside Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara has been prosecuted in Moroccan courts, as the December 2005 trial of seven human-rights defenders shows, with Human Rights Watch calling the charges against them dubious.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no trans-specific sourcing for this territory. Nothing is sourced on identity documents or gender markers, entry and visa screening, airport or custody screening, bathroom and facilities rules, healthcare or transition-care access, hate-crime protection, or recognition of a partner or marriage. These areas are unresolved rather than absent from the territory's law.

No trans-specific violence or killing figure with a denominator is available for Western Sahara, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made and none is asserted.

The sources do not map which parts of the territory stand under which framework, and they do not establish whether Moroccan statute extends to the territory by formal legal instrument or is applied through control on the ground. The 2005 trial and the 2009 camp-detention finding are historical; the dossier holds no current enforcement data for either.
